Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Data Scientist
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Affective Expression: Crying
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Vignette:
Mateo, a 25-year-old data scientist, remembers the day his younger sister, Sofia, became critically ill with a sudden, aggressive infection as a series of fragmented, terrifying snapshots rather than a coherent narrative. One moment, Sofia was complaining of a headache; the next, she was convulsing, her small body rigid. The frantic 911 call, the blaring sirens of the ambulance arriving at their apartment building, the smell of his own fear-induced sweat mingling with the paramedics’ hurried movements in their cramped living room – these sensations are seared into his memory. He recalls Sofia’s weak, whimpering cries during the chaotic ride to the hospital, and then the chilling silence as she was rushed into the emergency room, intubated, her life hanging by a thread. The sheer intensity of that time, the feeling of utter helplessness, was so extreme that now, when Mateo tries to recount the events, he often feels like the story is unreal, as if it happened to someone else or was a vivid, horrifying dream. He finds himself unable to put the memories of the event in the right order, the sequence jumbled and elusive, yet any attempt to recall it brings back the same visceral terror he felt at the time, his heart pounding, his breath catching in his throat.

In the months that followed Sofia’s eventual recovery, Mateo found himself living in a constant state of hypervigilance. Ordinary sounds, like a sudden clatter in his office or a car horn blaring outside his apartment in the city, make him jump violently, his entire body tensing as if bracing for another emergency. Sleep offers little respite; he often lies awake for hours, struggling to fall asleep because he feels an inexplicable need to stay alert, a vague sense that he must be ready for something terrible to happen again. This constant vigilance leaves him perpetually exhausted. When something does remind him of that stressful experience—a distant siren wailing, the faint scent of disinfectant from a passing hospital visitor, or the sound of a child crying in the park—he experiences strong physical reactions: his palms sweat, his heart races, and a cold knot forms in his stomach.

To cope, Mateo developed a rigid set of strategies. He spends increasingly long hours at his job as a data scientist, immersing himself in complex algorithms and datasets. This intense focus is, in part, a deliberate effort to suppress thoughts about the trauma; he tries hard not to think about Sofia’s illness, immediately diverting his attention whenever a memory threatens to surface. He has also become meticulous about never allowing himself to feel or express anger, believing it to be a dangerous or unproductive emotion, a lesson perhaps learned from the overwhelming frustration he felt when unable to help Sofia. This suppression extends to his personal life, where he often internalizes his frustrations, leading to a quiet, withdrawn demeanor.

His avoidance extends to anything remotely connected to medical settings. He takes circuitous routes to work to avoid driving past the hospital where Sofia was treated, adding significant time to his commute. He has put off his annual physical examination for over a year, despite gentle nudges from his family, because the thought of stepping into a doctor’s office fills him with an overwhelming sense of dread. These avoidance behaviors, combined with his constant exhaustion and the emotional distance he maintains, have started to take a toll. He feels increasingly isolated, and the emotional effort required to keep the memories and fears at bay is immense. Mateo is now seeking help because the relentless anxiety and the profound sense of exhaustion have become unbearable; he fears that if he continues this way, the terror he’s been fighting so hard to contain will eventually consume him entirely.
